section_summary: This section contains the end of a translated proposal for dispersing Japanese industry, followed by four translated Japanese periodical articles enclosed with an American Embassy despatch from Chungking. The articles discuss cabinet policy and wartime production, the resources of North China, Japan’s industrial and transport problems, and the mobilization of women and students for labor. The final article continues beyond page 141.

subfiles.title: Proposal for new industrial construction zones and a national industrial plan
subfiles.doc_type: translated article or report, concluding pages
subfiles.about: The concluding pages propose dispersed industrial zones and a national plan for wartime production.
subfiles.summary: The text classifies industrial zones and calls for regional planning that accounts for materials, labor, power, transport, markets, and defense.

subfiles.title: What Is Expected of the New Cabinet
subfiles.doc_type: translated symposium article, enclosure no. 6 to despatch no. 259
subfiles.from: Toyo Keizai (The Oriental Economy); translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.to: F.E.A.; O.W.I., American Embassy, and OSS for information
subfiles.about: Japanese commentators discuss what a new wartime cabinet should do after Tojo’s resignation.
subfiles.summary: The speakers urge rapid increases in aircraft and munitions production, better access to resources and labor, and changes to taxation and inflation policy. Several call for freer public discussion, stronger political organization, clearer cabinet responsibility, and closer coordination with military headquarters. Komigiwa criticizes food distribution, labor conscription, price controls, and wasteful uses of resources.

subfiles.title: Re-valuation of the Natural Resources of North China
subfiles.from: Toa (East Asia); translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.about: The article argues for developing North China’s resources as a nearby supply base for Japanese industry.
subfiles.summary: The article presents North China as a source of coal, iron, alumina shale, salt, and cotton that could support Japanese war production despite transport difficulties. It contrasts North and South China, surveys estimates of mineral reserves, and argues that industrial development depends on Japanese capital, machinery, and technical support. Its final page discusses bauxite deposits and an irrigation project.

subfiles.title: A General Survey of Economics (Extracts)
subfiles.doc_type: translated magazine article, enclosure no. 8 to despatch no. 259
subfiles.from: Nihon Hyoron (The Japan Critic); translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.to: F.E.A.; O.W.I. and American Embassy for information
subfiles.about: The extracts review Japanese wartime production, resources, transport, air raid preparations, and urban food supply.
subfiles.summary: The article describes concentrating labor, machinery, and materials on aircraft production while seeking more coal and iron. It proposes factory groups to shift work after air raids and outlines emergency transport headquarters, railway performance, and priority movement of aircraft materials. It also sets out labor measures during air raids and special food distributions for major cities.

subfiles.title: The State of Labor Mobilization
subfiles.doc_type: translated weekly report, enclosure no. 9 to despatch no. 259
subfiles.from: Weekly report published in Tokyo; translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center
subfiles.to: F.E.A.; OSS and American Embassy for information
subfiles.about: A question-and-answer report explains Japan’s expanded mobilization of women and students for war work.
subfiles.summary: The report explains selection, exemptions, service terms, penalties, workplace conditions, and proposed duties for the women’s labor force. It then presents student labor as part of education, describes employers’ responsibilities, and begins listing changes to student mobilization rules. The document continues beyond page 141.
